findings.title: Federated recovery-codes credential never removed when all codes are used
findings.body: When a user has recovery codes stored in federated storage and all codes have been consumed, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. `removeStoredCredentialById` only acts on credentials in local Keycloak storage, not on federated credentials returned via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. The result is that the (now exhausted) credential remains in the user storage and is still picked up by `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` on subsequent logins, so the user is repeatedly asked to re-configure while the stale credential is never cleaned up. There must be a separate path (or a fallback to a federated-credential delete) when the credential was returned from the user storage.

findings.title: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean crashes if user has no recovery codes
findings.body: The constructor does `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(credentialModelOpt.get())` directly on the result of `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)`, which returns `Optional<CredentialModel>`. If the user has never configured recovery codes (e.g. the bean is rendered for a user in any context where they don't exist), `get()` throws `java.util.NoSuchElementException` and the login template fails to render. This was safe before the change because the previous code used `findFirst().get()` on the local-credentials stream and would throw a similar error, but the new code now also considers federated credentials and the same fragility remains; an explicit `isPresent()` check (and a sensible fallback when absent) is required.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored and compared in plaintext in user storage
findings.body: `updateCredential` stores `input.getChallengeResponse()` (the raw codes JSON) directly in `credentialData`, and `isValid` reads it back and does `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. Recovery codes are intended to be one-time, low-trust-secret recovery material and the local Keycloak provider stores them hashed (via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode`). Storing them as plaintext and comparing raw-vs-raw in the user-storage SPI means a breach of this user storage yields every still-valid recovery code in cleartext, and provides a copy-paste template that propagates this insecure pattern to real user-storage implementations. The `isValid` path should normalize through the same hash used by the local provider, and the stored credential data should be hashed at rest.

findings.title: getCredentials returns a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel with a regenerated id
findings.body: `getCredentials` constructs the returned `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(rawCodes, createdDate, userLabel)`, which does not take the existing `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()`. Every time the credential is listed, a new id is generated. Downstream consumers that try to manage the credential by id — including the new `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` — then operate on a non-existent local-storage id, so any per-id operation (remove, update, disable) against the federated credential silently no-ops. `getCredentials` should return a model whose `getId()` equals `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()`.

findings.title: New recovery-codes integration test covers only one happy path
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` exercises exactly one successful login with the first requested recovery code. It does not cover: (a) reusing the same code a second time (must fail), (b) entering an invalid code (must fail with the configured error), (c) using every code in sequence until `allCodesUsed()` triggers the required action and removes the credential (the path the diff actually changed), or (d) disabling the recovery-codes credential via the admin REST. The cleanup/id-mismatch bug noted above would not be caught by this test because the all-codes-used branch is never reached.
